questions.stem:
A 6-year-old girl who has never been vaccinated returns from a long visit with relatives abroad with 3 days of sore throat, low-grade fever, and a hoarse voice. Her neck is swollen. A gray, adherent membrane covers both tonsils and the posterior pharynx, and it bleeds when scraped. Gram stain of material beneath the membrane shows gram-positive rods. An electrocardiogram shows new conduction abnormalities.

In addition to an antibiotic such as penicillin, which treatment should she receive?
choices: Intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose aspirin
Inactivated whole-cell vaccine given today in clinic
Oral rifampin for 4 days for her and her household
Antitoxin directed at the bacterial exotoxin
Vitamin A supplementation

explain.html: Diphtheria is a toxin-mediated disease caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae, an aerobic gram-positive rod acquired in the nasopharynx. Its exotoxin inhibits cellular protein synthesis and destroys local tissue, most often in the pharynx and tonsils, producing an adherent pseudomembrane. The toxin also reaches distant organs, and myocarditis is the most frequent fatal complication; death occurs in 5 to 10%. This unvaccinated girl, back from abroad, has a gray membrane over the tonsils that bleeds when scraped, gram-positive rods, a swollen neck, and new conduction abnormalities on ECG, which signal cardiac toxin effect. Because the toxin does the damage, treatment is diphtheria antitoxin to neutralize it plus penicillin (or erythromycin) to clear the organism, and the DTaP series prevents it.

FeatureDiphtheriaTetanusPertussis
OrganismCorynebacterium diphtheriae, aerobic gram-positive rodClostridium tetani, anaerobic gram-positive spore formerBordetella pertussis, attaches to respiratory cilia
Toxin actionInhibits protein synthesis, destroys local tissueBlocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNSPrimarily toxin mediated
HallmarkPharyngeal pseudomembrane; myocarditis is the top fatal complicationTrismus, rigidity, spasmsParoxysmal cough, whoop, post-tussive vomiting; apnea in infants
Treatment or preventionAntitoxin plus penicillin (or erythromycin)DTaP and TdapAzithromycin for patient and contacts; Tdap in every pregnancy
why: Immunoglobulin with aspirin treats Kawasaki disease, a vasculitis, not a toxin-producing infection.
Vaccinating during active disease does not neutralize the toxin already causing damage.
Rifampin is the prophylaxis for contacts of invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b disease.
Vitamin A improves outcomes in measles, not diphtheria.
explain.takeaway: Diphtheria (pharyngeal pseudomembrane, myocarditis as the leading fatal complication) is caused by an exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis and is treated with antitoxin plus penicillin or erythromycin.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Recognize clinical manifestations and impact of specific vaccine preventable bacterial diseases

questions.stem:
A 45-year-old farmer stepped on a rusty nail in his barn 10 days ago and did not seek care. His last vaccine of any kind was in childhood. He now has jaw stiffness so severe he cannot open his mouth, a stiff neck, trouble swallowing, and a board-like abdomen. Loud noises trigger painful generalized spasms. He is fully alert.

The toxin responsible for his symptoms acts by which of the following mechanisms?
choices: Inhibiting protein synthesis in muscle fibers
Blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release centrally
Destroying motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord
Cross-linking T cell receptors to MHC class II molecules
Binding the acetylcholine receptor at the motor end plate

explain.html: Tetanus is caused by the exotoxin of Clostridium tetani, an anaerobic gram-positive spore-forming rod whose spores live in soil and resist heat and antiseptics. The pathogenesis runs in order: spores enter through a wound, germinate in anaerobic conditions, and produce toxin, which binds in the central nervous system and interferes with neurotransmitter release so that inhibitory impulses are blocked. Without inhibition, muscles contract unopposed, giving trismus (lockjaw), neck stiffness, difficulty swallowing, abdominal rigidity, and convulsive spasms that continue for 3 to 4 weeks. The incubation is 8 to 21 days. This farmer has a puncture wound 10 days ago, no boosters since childhood, lockjaw, a board-like abdomen, and spasms triggered by noise while fully alert. The tetanus component of DTaP and Tdap prevents it.
explain.table:
FeatureDiphtheriaTetanusPertussis
OrganismCorynebacterium diphtheriae, aerobic gram-positive rodClostridium tetani, anaerobic gram-positive spore formerBordetella pertussis, attaches to respiratory cilia
Toxin actionInhibits protein synthesis, destroys local tissueBlocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNSPrimarily toxin mediated
HallmarkPharyngeal pseudomembrane; myocarditis is the top fatal complicationTrismus, rigidity, spasmsParoxysmal cough, whoop, post-tussive vomiting; apnea in infants
Treatment or preventionAntitoxin plus penicillin (or erythromycin)DTaP and TdapAzithromycin for patient and contacts; Tdap in every pregnancy
why: Inhibiting protein synthesis is the action of diphtheria toxin, which causes a pseudomembrane and myocarditis.
Destroying anterior horn motor neurons is the poliovirus lesion, which causes flaccid, not rigid, paralysis.
Cross-linking T cell receptors to MHC class II is the superantigen action of toxic shock toxins.
Blocking the acetylcholine receptor at the end plate would cause weakness, not rigidity and spasm.
explain.takeaway: Tetanus toxin binds in the central nervous system and blocks release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing unopposed muscle contraction: trismus, rigidity, and spasms.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Recognize clinical manifestations and impact of specific vaccine preventable bacterial diseases

rows.if_right: a pharyngeal pseudomembrane with gram-positive rods and new heart block

questions.stem:
A 16-year-old healthy girl comes for a routine visit. She received one dose of the quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine against serogroups A, C, W, and Y at age 11. She plans to live in a college dormitory in 2 years. Her mother asks why another meningococcal dose is needed when she was already vaccinated.

Which of the following best explains the recommendation for a booster at this age?
choices: The first dose did not cover serogroup Y
Protection wanes, and the risk peaks in later adolescence
The first dose is given only to prime the response to serogroup B
A booster is required only for travel to the African meningitis belt
A booster is needed only if she has a late complement deficiency

explain.html: Neisseria meningitidis is an aerobic gram-negative bacterium whose polysaccharide capsule defines its serogroups, and almost all invasive disease is caused by A, B, C, W, X, and Y. The MenACWY vaccine covers A, C, W, and Y; MenB covers B, which causes about a third of US cases and is the most common cause in adolescents. Vaccine effectiveness is about 91% in the first year but falls to about 58% at 2 to 5 years, because protection wanes. So all adolescents receive MenACWY at 11 to 12 and a booster at 16, which covers the ages when adolescents are at highest risk. This girl got her dose at 11 and will be in a college dorm at 18, squarely in that window. MenB is offered by shared decision at 16 to 23 and is required by many colleges, and high-risk patients get extra series and frequent boosters.

MenBBShared decision at 16 to 23 (preferred 16 to 18); many colleges require it
MenABCWYA, B, C, W, YCombined option

MenACWY does not prime for serogroup B, which needs a separate MenB vaccine.
The booster at 16 is routine for all adolescents, not only travelers.
Late complement deficiency calls for a more intense schedule, but the booster at 16 is for everyone.
explain.takeaway: MenACWY is given at 11 to 12 with a booster at 16 because effectiveness falls from about 91% to 58% within a few years, and risk peaks in late adolescence.

explain.objective: Become familiar with recommended routine vaccination schedule for newborns through18 years of age

questions.stem:
A public health student reviews US polio cases. After a live oral vaccine containing all three serotypes was introduced in 1963, wild virus transmission ended, with the last endemic case in 1979. By the late 1990s, however, nearly all remaining paralytic polio cases in the US were linked to the vaccine itself. In 2000 the US switched to a different vaccine and these cases stopped.

Which property of the earlier vaccine explains both its benefit and the problem it caused?
choices: Inactivated virus that had to be given by injection
Only one of the three poliovirus serotypes was included
Antibodies were made in the blood but not in the gut
A recombinant viral surface protein made in the laboratory
Live virus shed in stool that rarely caused paralysis

explain.html: Poliovirus is a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA enterovirus with 3 serotypes, spread fecal-orally; it replicates in the oropharynx and small intestine, reaches the CNS through the blood, and destroys anterior horn motor neurons, causing flaccid paralysis. The live attenuated oral polio vaccine, trivalent and the US vaccine of choice after 1963, is shed in stool for up to 6 weeks, which spreads vaccine virus to contacts and produced herd immunity; the last endemic wild case in the US was in 1979. The same live virus rarely causes vaccine-associated paralytic polio (VAPP), and by 1999, 95% of US polio cases were VAPP. To eliminate VAPP, the US switched to inactivated polio vaccine exclusively in 2000; IPV makes more than 99% of recipients immune after 3 doses. The student's timeline, success followed by vaccine-linked paralysis, matches that live, shed virus.

HPVRecombinant L1 virus-like particles11 to 12 years (from 9), catch-up through 26
MMR, varicellaLive attenuated12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years
Hepatitis AInactivated whole virus2 doses from 12 months
why: The earlier vaccine was live and oral; inactivated injected vaccine is what replaced it.
The oral vaccine contained all three serotypes, not one.
Gut immunity and spread to contacts were strengths of the oral vaccine, not its weakness.
A recombinant surface protein describes the hepatitis B vaccine antigen, not polio vaccine.
explain.takeaway: Live oral polio vaccine is shed in stool, giving herd immunity but rarely causing vaccine-associated paralytic polio, so the US has used only inactivated polio vaccine since 2000.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Recognize the impact of vaccines on disease prevention in the pediatric population

questions.stem:
An 18-week-old boy is seen for his first well visit since birth; the family missed the 2-month visit after a move. He is healthy and growing well. The clinician reviews the live oral vaccine that protects against the most common cause of severe watery diarrhea, dehydration, and metabolic acidosis in infants, a segmented double-stranded RNA virus that replicates in the small intestinal epithelium.

Which of the following is correct about this vaccine for this infant?
choices: Give the first dose today and complete the series before 2 years
Do not start it; the first dose must come before 15 weeks
Give it only after he turns 12 months, with the measles vaccine
Give an inactivated injectable form instead of the oral vaccine
Start the series today, because there is no upper age limit

explain.html: Rotavirus is a segmented double-stranded RNA virus of the Reoviridae family, spread fecal-orally, that replicates in small intestinal epithelium. It is the most common cause of severe diarrhea in infants and children, with dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and metabolic acidosis; before the vaccine nearly every child was infected by age 5, with more than 500,000 diarrheal deaths a year worldwide. The vaccine is a live oral vaccine given routinely to all infants, and it has strict age limits: the first dose must come before 15 weeks of age, and all doses should be finished before 8 months. This 18-week-old missed the 2-month visit, so he is past the window to start the series even though he is healthy.

questions.stem:
A 12-year-old boy comes for his routine adolescent visit. His father asks how the human papillomavirus vaccine can protect against cancer if it does not contain any virus that can infect cells. The clinician explains that the vaccine is made by recombinant technology from one viral protein that assembles by itself into a particle that looks like the virus.

Which of the following best describes the vaccine antigen and how it protects?
choices: E6 and E7 oncoproteins that teach T cells to kill tumor cells
Live attenuated virus that establishes a harmless latent infection
L1 capsid protein particles that induce neutralizing antibodies
Killed whole virus that is effective even in people already infected
A capsular polysaccharide linked to a carrier protein

explain.html: Human papillomavirus is a small double-stranded DNA virus; types 16 and 18 cause about 70% of cervical cancers and many other anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers, and types 6 and 11 cause about 90% of genital warts. The vaccine antigen is L1, the major capsid protein, made by recombinant technology. L1 proteins self-assemble into virus-like particles that look like the virus to the immune system but are noninfectious and non-oncogenic because they carry no viral DNA, and they induce antibodies that block infection by vaccine types. The 9-valent vaccine includes 16, 18, 6, and 11. Because it prevents infection rather than treating it, there is no evidence of efficacy against a vaccine type already acquired, which is why it is given routinely at 11 to 12, before exposure, with catch-up through 26.

explain.takeaway: The HPV vaccine is recombinant L1 capsid protein that self-assembles into noninfectious virus-like particles inducing neutralizing antibody; it prevents but does not treat infection with vaccine types.

questions.stem:
A healthy 12-month-old girl is due for her first doses of the live attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine and the varicella vaccine. Her mother asks whether one combined injection of all four (MMRV) is better than two separate injections at the same visit. The clinician reviews data showing about 8 febrile seizures per 10,000 children aged 12 to 23 months after the combined product, compared with about 4 per 10,000 after separate MMR and varicella vaccines given the same day.

Which recommendation fits these data?
choices: Delay both vaccines until she is 4 years old
Give separate MMR and varicella vaccines for this first dose
Give MMR now and varicella only after age 13
Give the combined vaccine, as seizures are equally common
Give only the measles component now, the rest at 18 months

explain.html: Measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella vaccines are live attenuated virus vaccines with a minimum age of 12 months, given in 2 doses at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years. A combined MMRV product exists, but in young toddlers the first dose carries a higher febrile seizure risk: about 8 per 10,000 after MMRV at 12 to 23 months versus 4 per 10,000 after MMR and varicella given separately at the same visit. For that reason, between 12 and 47 months, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are suggested for the first dose. This 12-month-old is due for both, and the data her clinician quotes are exactly that comparison. Delaying vaccination is not the answer, since it leaves her unprotected against measles and varicella.
why: Delaying both vaccines leaves her unprotected against measles and varicella during the years of exposure.
Varicella vaccine is given routinely at 12 to 15 months, with no reason to wait until adolescence.
The data show twice as many febrile seizures after the combined product, so they are not equal.
MMR is a single combined vaccine and is not split into components.
explain.takeaway: For the first dose at 12 to 47 months, separate MMR and varicella vaccines are suggested because MMRV doubles febrile seizure risk (about 8 versus 4 per 10,000).
explain.topic: MMR and varicella: febrile seizure risk
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Become familiar with recommended routine vaccination schedule for newborns through18 years of age

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit in October. Her first child was hospitalized at 2 months of age with wheezing, fast breathing, and low oxygen from inflammation of the small airways during the winter. She asks what can be done to protect the new baby from the same virus this season.

Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?
choices: A single dose of RSV vaccine for her now, at 32 to 36 weeks
Tdap for her now, since it prevents bronchiolitis in infants
Live attenuated nasal influenza vaccine for the newborn at birth
Two doses of RSV vaccine for the infant at 2 and 4 months
No option, since immunity to the virus cannot be given to infants

explain.html: Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in young children, inflaming the small airways and causing serious breathing difficulty, especially in infants, premature babies, and children with underlying conditions. The older child's winter hospitalization at 2 months fits RSV bronchiolitis. Young infants are protected passively. Pregnant people should receive a single dose of RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks, and in most of the US the vaccine is given from September through January, so maternal antibody protects the newborn through the season. If the mother does not receive it, a monoclonal antibody is available for the newborn. This woman is at 34 weeks in October, inside both windows, so a single dose now is the plan.

Vaccine in pregnancyTimingProtects the infant against

Influenza vaccine starts at 6 months and does not prevent RSV.
The RSV strategy is maternal vaccination or an infant monoclonal antibody, not an infant vaccine series.
Infants can be protected passively, through maternal vaccination or a monoclonal antibody.
explain.takeaway: Newborns are protected from RSV by a single maternal RSV vaccine dose at 32 to 36 weeks during the season (September to January), or by a monoclonal antibody if the mother was not vaccinated.
explain.topic: RSV: maternal vaccine or infant monoclonal antibody

questions.stem:
A healthy 4-year-old girl comes in September for her first-ever influenza vaccine; her parents had declined it in prior years. She has no allergies. The clinician explains that the inactivated injectable vaccine protects against influenza A and B, and that young children with influenza can develop otitis media, croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and neurologic complications.

Which schedule is recommended for her this season?
choices: One dose now, then a dose every 5 years
No dose, since vaccination starts at age 5
Two doses during this first season
One dose now, with no further doses needed
A single dose only if she has asthma

explain.html: Influenza viruses (orthomyxoviruses) cause sudden fever with cough, chills, myalgia, headache, and malaise; infants can present with a nonspecific sepsis-like illness, and children under 5, especially under 1, develop otitis media, croup, bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and neurologic complications. The vaccine protects against types A and B and comes as an injectable inactivated form or a live attenuated nasal spray. Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual flu vaccine, especially children under 5 and children of any age with a high-risk condition. Children under 8 need 2 doses in their first year of vaccination. This healthy 4-year-old is receiving influenza vaccine for the first time ever, so she needs two doses this season and one each year after.

Vaccination starts at 6 months, not 5 years.
A single dose is enough only for children previously vaccinated or aged 8 and older.
Annual vaccination is recommended for all children 6 months and older, not only those with asthma.
explain.takeaway: Annual influenza vaccine is recommended for everyone 6 months and older, and children under 8 receiving it for the first time need 2 doses that first season.

questions.stem:
A 5-week-old girl is admitted with episodes in which she stops breathing and turns blue. For 2 weeks she had a runny nose and mild cough, then bursts of rapid coughing followed by vomiting. Her father has had a cough for 6 weeks that he calls a lingering cold. A nasopharyngeal specimen grows a small gram-negative coccobacillus. Her mother received no vaccines during pregnancy.

Which intervention would most likely have prevented this infant's illness?
choices: A dose of pertussis vaccine for the infant at birth
Oral rifampin for the father once his cough began
The 2-month DTaP dose given 3 weeks early
Annual inactivated influenza vaccine for the mother
Tdap for the mother at 27 to 36 weeks of each pregnancy

explain.html: Pertussis (whooping cough) from Bordetella pertussis is a toxin-mediated disease: the bacteria attach to the cilia of respiratory epithelium and spread through respiratory secretions with attack rates of 80 to 90%. It starts as an upper respiratory infection (catarrhal stage), progresses to paroxysms of cough with an inspiratory whoop followed by vomiting, and wanes over weeks to months. Infants have the most dangerous complications: apnea in 61%, hypoxia, seizures, pneumonia, and pulmonary hypertension, the most fatal. Adolescents and adults lose immunity without boosting and become the reservoir, exactly like this father with a 6-week cough. Because infants are too young to receive the pertussis vaccine, the protection comes from a single dose of Tdap during every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks, which this mother did not receive.

questions.stem:
A 14-month-old boy whose parents declined all vaccines has fever, irritability, a bulging fontanelle, and neck stiffness. Spinal fluid shows many neutrophils, low glucose, and small pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli. The organism grows on chocolate agar but not on blood agar unless certain supplements are added. He has a 3-year-old sister at home who is also unvaccinated.

The organism requires which growth factors, and what should the sister receive?
choices: Factors V and X; rifampin for 4 days
Cysteine and iron; oral doxycycline
Factors V and X; oral azithromycin for 5 days
Cholesterol; a single dose of penicillin
Cysteine and iron; ceftriaxone for 10 days

explain.html: Haemophilus influenzae is an aerobic gram-negative bacterium with a polysaccharide capsule in six serotypes (a to f); type b caused 95% of invasive disease before the vaccine, and it was the leading cause of bacterial meningitis then. Meningitis is the most common Hib disease (50 to 65%), and the mnemonic HaEMOPhilus recalls epiglottitis, meningitis, otitis media, and pneumonia. In the lab it grows on chocolate agar because it needs factor V (NAD+) and factor X (hematin). This unvaccinated toddler has meningitis with small gram-negative coccobacilli that grow only on chocolate agar. Disease requires 10 days of IV antibiotics, while unimmunized close contacts such as household and day care members receive rifampin for 4 days, so his unvaccinated sister qualifies. Routine Hib vaccination at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months has cut incidence by 99%.
explain.table:
Index caseContacts who receive prophylaxisDrug
Invasive HibUnimmunized close contacts (household, day care)Rifampin for 4 days
Invasive meningococcal diseaseHousehold, child care, anyone exposed to oral secretionsRifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone
PertussisAll family members and close contactsAzithromycin
why: Cysteine and iron are not the Hib growth requirements, and doxycycline is not Hib prophylaxis.
The growth factors are right, but azithromycin is the prophylaxis for pertussis contacts, not Hib.
Haemophilus does not need cholesterol, and penicillin is not the prophylaxis for Hib contacts.
Cysteine and iron are wrong, and a 10-day IV course is treatment of disease, not prophylaxis.
explain.takeaway: Haemophilus influenzae grows on chocolate agar because it needs factors V (NAD+) and X (hematin); unimmunized close contacts of invasive Hib disease receive rifampin for 4 days.

questions.stem:
Investigators compare two pneumococcal vaccines in healthy 6-month-old infants. Vaccine 1 contains purified capsular polysaccharide from 23 serotypes. Vaccine 2 contains capsular polysaccharide from fewer serotypes chemically linked to a nontoxic diphtheria toxin protein. Four weeks after the series, infants given vaccine 1 have barely detectable capsule-specific antibody and no rise after a later booster, while infants given vaccine 2 have high titers of class-switched IgG and a strong booster response.

Which of the following best explains the response to vaccine 2?
choices: Infants make more polysaccharide-specific IgM than adults
Diphtheria toxin directly activates B cells as a superantigen
The polysaccharide is presented on MHC class I to CD8 T cells
The carrier recruits helper T cells for switching and memory
Linkage to protein raises antibody only against diphtheria toxin

explain.html: The polysaccharide capsule is the key virulence factor of Streptococcus pneumoniae, and type-specific antibody against it is protective. Two kinds of vaccine target it. The 23-valent purified polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23, Pneumovax) contains capsule alone, and it is not effective in children under 2, as vaccine 1 shows here. The conjugate vaccines (PCV15, PCV20, PCV21) link capsular polysaccharide to a nontoxic diphtheria toxin protein (CRM197), which makes them highly immunogenic in infants, more than 90% effective against invasive disease, and the basis of the routine 4-dose series at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months. The protein carrier is what changes the response: it brings in helper T cells, which drive class switching to IgG and memory, explaining vaccine 2's high IgG titers and strong booster response in these 6-month-olds.
explain.table:
FeaturePPSV23 (Pneumovax)PCV15, PCV20, PCV21
AntigenPurified capsular polysaccharide from 23 typesCapsular polysaccharide conjugated to nontoxic diphtheria toxin (CRM197)
Children under 2Not effectiveHighly immunogenic, including high-risk children
UseAdults and high-risk patients, after a PCVRoutine 4-dose series at 2, 4, 6, and 12 to 15 months
EffectivenessNot the infant vaccineOver 90% against invasive disease, less against pneumonia and otitis
why: Young infants respond poorly to polysaccharide alone, so a larger IgM response does not explain the result.
CRM197 is a nontoxic carrier protein, not a superantigen, and superantigens do not make specific antibody.
Polysaccharides are not presented on MHC class I; carrier peptides go to helper T cells on MHC class II.
The key result is high antibody against the capsule, the part that protects against pneumococcus.
explain.takeaway: Conjugating pneumococcal capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier (CRM197) recruits helper T cells, so conjugate vaccines work in infants while plain polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) fails before age 2.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Become familiar with recommended routine vaccination schedule for newborns through18 years of age

questions.stem:
A woman delivers a healthy term boy. Her prenatal labs show the following.

[[labs 0]]

Without intervention, most infants in this situation become infected, and nearly all of those infected become chronic carriers at risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Which of the following should the newborn receive within hours of birth?
choices: Hepatitis B vaccine alone, with a second dose at 1 month
Hepatitis B immune globulin alone, with vaccine at 2 months
Inactivated hepatitis A vaccine together with immune globulin
Hepatitis B vaccine plus immune globulin, at separate sites
No intervention until the infant's own surface antigen is checked

explain.html: Hepatitis B is a partially double-stranded DNA hepadnavirus spread by blood and body fluids, including perinatal transmission. Infant risk depends on the mother's markers: if she is HBsAg positive and HBeAg positive (chronically infected and highly infectious), 70 to 90% of infants are infected, versus about 10% when only HBsAg is positive. About 90% of infected infants become chronically infected, and hepatitis B causes chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and about 80% of hepatocellular carcinomas. The vaccine is recombinant HBsAg, and every medically stable newborn of an HBsAg-negative mother receives a dose within 24 hours. When the mother is HBsAg positive, as here, the infant gets hepatitis B vaccine plus hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) in separate limbs within 12 hours, combining immediate passive protection with active immunity.
why: Vaccine alone is the plan when the mother is HBsAg negative; this infant also needs immune globulin.
Immune globulin without vaccine gives only temporary protection and delays active immunity.
Hepatitis A vaccine does not protect against hepatitis B and starts at 12 months.
Waiting lets infection establish; prevention must start at birth.
explain.takeaway: Newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers receive hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG at separate sites within 12 hours of birth, because up to 90% would otherwise be infected and most would become chronic carriers.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Become familiar with recommended routine vaccination schedule for newborns through18 years of age

questions.stem:
A 9-year-old boy has had 6 months of falling grades, personality change, and clumsiness, and now has sudden jerking movements of his arms several times a day. Spinal fluid shows very high levels of antibody against a virus. As an unvaccinated 8-month-old living abroad, he had an illness with high fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, followed by a rash that began on his face and spread downward.

Which of the following would have been the most effective way to prevent this outcome?
choices: Acyclovir given at the time of the infant rash
Two doses of a live attenuated childhood vaccine
Inactivated polio vaccine given in the first year of life
Rifampin prophylaxis given right after his infant illness
Hepatitis B vaccine given within 24 hours of birth

explain.html: Measles is an enveloped RNA Morbillivirus that starts with 2 to 4 days of high fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, then a rash that begins on the face and spreads down. Its complications range from otitis media, pneumonia, croup, and diarrhea to acute encephalitis in about 1 per 1,000. The latest is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare degenerative CNS disease with behavioral and intellectual deterioration and seizures that appears 7 to 10 years after measles, especially when measles occurred in infancy. This boy had measles at 8 months abroad and now has falling grades, personality change, myoclonic jerks, and high spinal fluid antibody to the virus. There is no antiviral that prevents it; prevention is the live attenuated MMR vaccine in two doses, at 12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 years, with an early dose from 6 months for outbreaks or travel.
why: Acyclovir targets herpesviruses and has no effect on measles virus.
Polio vaccine does not protect against measles.
Rifampin is antibacterial prophylaxis with no effect on a virus.
Hepatitis B vaccine prevents hepatitis B, not measles.
explain.takeaway: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis is a fatal degenerative CNS complication 7 to 10 years after measles, most often after infection in infancy, prevented by two doses of MMR.
explain.subject: Immunology
explain.objective: Understand possible complications of infections with vaccine preventable diseases in childhood
